path.title: SQL and data semantics
path.summary: Rows first: joins, filters, aggregation and window frames.

lessons.title: Join rows, not circles
lessons.summary: Match keys, preserve unmatched rows, and see why duplicates multiply.

blocks.title: The mental model
blocks.body: A table can contain duplicate keys. Every matching pair contributes a row. Choose INNER, LEFT, FULL, SEMI or ANTI in the visual. The fixture is fully visible; it is not your SQL execution.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.body: A Venn diagram hides row multiplicity. Before summing a joined amount, verify the relationship cardinality.

blocks.title: Before you run
blocks.body: Predict the LEFT JOIN row count. Then compare with INNER, FULL, SEMI and ANTI.

visual.title: Join rows, not circles - visual walkthrough

steps.title: Match keys
steps.body: A join tests pairs of rows. Equal non-null keys match.

steps.title: Preserve rows
steps.body: LEFT keeps unmatched left rows with nulls for the right-hand columns.

steps.title: Count the result
steps.body: Two orders for Ada create two output rows. A join is not set intersection.

steps.title: Null keys
steps.body: With ordinary equality, a null key does not match another null key.

lessons.title: LEFT JOIN: ON versus WHERE
lessons.summary: Keep the customer even when no order satisfies the filter.

blocks.title: The mental model
blocks.body: The same predicate has different consequences in ON and WHERE. Use the visual filter placement control, then edit the SQL file in Try. The Watch fixture does not silently rewrite your file.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.body: WHERE o.status = DONE removes unmatched customers. This does not mean every WHERE predicate turns a LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN; the predicate must reject the null-extended rows.

blocks.title: Before you run
blocks.body: Which customers disappear when the DONE predicate moves into WHERE?

visual.title: LEFT JOIN: ON versus WHERE - visual walkthrough

steps.title: Filter candidate matches
steps.body: A right-side condition in ON restricts which rows can match.

steps.title: Add unmatched rows
steps.body: The LEFT JOIN still preserves customers with no qualifying match.

steps.title: Move it to WHERE
steps.body: WHERE is evaluated after the join. A null right-side status fails status = DONE.

steps.title: Repair the query
steps.body: Move right-side eligibility conditions back into ON when left preservation is required.

lessons.title: GROUP BY and HAVING
lessons.summary: Change the grain deliberately and filter groups after aggregation.

blocks.title: The mental model
blocks.body: Write down what one input row represents and what one output row represents. This query changes the grain from order to customer segment. The real example uses the existing local source.orders seed.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.body: Filtering positive orders before SUM is not the same as filtering groups with a positive net total after SUM.

blocks.title: Before you run
blocks.body: Should a negative order be dropped, or should it reduce the segment total?

code.source:
SELECT segment_id, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(net_amount) AS revenue
FROM source.orders
GROUP BY segment_id
HAVING SUM(net_amount) > 100
ORDER BY segment_id;

visual.title: GROUP BY and HAVING - visual walkthrough

steps.title: Input grain
steps.body: source.orders contains one row per order.

steps.title: Group
steps.body: Rows with the same segment_id form one group.

steps.title: Aggregate
steps.body: SUM and COUNT reduce each group to one output row.

steps.title: Filter groups
steps.body: HAVING applies to aggregate results; WHERE filters individual input rows.

lessons.title: ROWS, RANGE and peer groups
lessons.summary: Move a window frame and inspect exactly which rows contribute.

blocks.title: The mental model
blocks.body: The visual fixture has two transactions on day 2. ROWS uses the deterministic order (day, txn_id). RANGE uses ORDER BY day, so both peers share the day total. The ordering difference is intentional and displayed.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.body: RANGE is not the same as counting a fixed number of rows. ROWS without a stable tie-breaker can make per-row results nondeterministic.

blocks.title: Before you run
blocks.body: At the first day-2 row, why is ROWS 70 while RANGE is 120?

visual.title: ROWS, RANGE and peer groups - visual walkthrough

steps.title: Keep the rows
steps.body: Unlike GROUP BY, a window adds a value without collapsing the result rows.

steps.title: Order deterministically
steps.body: ROWS uses positions. Include a stable tie-breaker when order matters.

steps.title: Inspect peers
steps.body: RANGE with ORDER BY day includes rows that share the current day.

steps.title: Check the frame
steps.body: The visual compares unbounded preceding to current row. It does not implement arbitrary SQL frames.

lessons.title: Know the grain of every row
lessons.summary: Say what one output row means, aggregate before joining to avoid fan-out, and spot subtotal rows that live at another grain.

blocks.title: One row means one what?
blocks.body: The grain is the end of the sentence "one row per ...". orders has one row per order; order lines have one row per order and product. Every GROUP BY declares the grain of its result: the GROUP BY columns become the key of the output. Write the sentence down before you write the query.

blocks.title: Fan-out
blocks.body: Joining orders (one row per order) to lines (several per order) repeats each order once per line. SUM(orders.shipping) after that join counts the shipping fee once per line. Aggregate the many side to the grain of the one side first, then join; or only sum columns that belong to the grain of the joined result.

blocks.title: Rows at several grains
blocks.body: GROUP BY ROLLUP(a, b) returns the detail rows (a, b), one subtotal per a with b set to NULL, and a grand total with both NULL. Those subtotal rows live at another grain: never add them up again with the detail rows. GROUPING(b) = 1 marks a row where b was rolled up, which tells a subtotal from a real NULL value.

blocks.title: Before you run
blocks.body: Predict the shipping total computed after the join to the lines, and after aggregating the lines first. Then add GROUP BY ROLLUP(status) to a query over orders and predict how many rows it returns.

code.source:
WITH orders(order_id, status, shipping) AS (
  VALUES (1, 'DONE', 10), (2, 'DONE', 6), (3, 'OPEN', 4)
), lines(order_id, product, amount) AS (
  VALUES (1, 'pen', 30), (1, 'ink', 70), (2, 'pad', 20), (3, 'pen', 15), (3, 'pad', 5)
), line_totals AS (
  SELECT order_id, SUM(amount) AS items, COUNT(*) AS line_count
  FROM lines
  GROUP BY order_id
)
SELECT
  (SELECT SUM(o.shipping) FROM orders o JOIN lines l USING (order_id)) AS shipping_fanned_out,
  SUM(o.shipping) AS shipping_correct,
  SUM(t.items) AS items_total
FROM orders o
JOIN line_totals t USING (order_id);

steps.title: Declare the grain
steps.body: orders: one row per order. lines: one row per order and product. line_totals: one row per order, because it groups by order_id.

steps.title: Watch the fan-out
steps.body: Joining orders to lines repeats an order once per line: shipping adds up to 34 instead of 20.

steps.title: Aggregate, then join
steps.body: line_totals is already at the order grain, so the join keeps one row per order and shipping adds up to 20.

steps.title: Subtotals are another grain
steps.body: ROLLUP adds subtotal and total rows to the result. Filter them with GROUPING() before you reuse the detail rows.

lessons.title: CTEs and subqueries: name each step
lessons.summary: Break a query into named steps with WITH, and know when a scalar, IN, EXISTS or correlated subquery is the clearer tool.

blocks.title: A CTE is a named query
blocks.body: WITH name AS (SELECT ...) defines a result you can read like a table in the rest of the statement. Each step gets a name and a grain, and you can build and check the steps one at a time. DuckDB usually inlines a CTE into the plan, so naming a step costs nothing; AS MATERIALIZED asks for it to be computed once.

blocks.title: Three kinds of subquery
blocks.body: A scalar subquery returns one value: (SELECT AVG(amount) FROM orders). IN (SELECT ...) and EXISTS (SELECT ...) test membership. A correlated subquery refers to the outer row (WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id): its meaning is "evaluated for each outer row", even when the optimizer turns it into a join.

blocks.title: NOT IN and NULL
blocks.body: x NOT IN (SELECT y FROM t) returns no row at all as soon as y contains a NULL, because x <> NULL is unknown rather than true. Use NOT EXISTS, or filter the NULLs out of the subquery.

blocks.title: Before you run
blocks.body: Predict which customers are above the global average order amount. Then set one amount to NULL and check that AVG ignores it.

code.source:
WITH orders(order_id, customer_id, amount) AS (
  VALUES (1, 'A', 40), (2, 'A', 60), (3, 'B', 20), (4, 'C', 90), (5, NULL, 10)
), global_avg AS (
  SELECT AVG(amount) AS avg_amount FROM orders
), per_customer AS (
  SELECT customer_id, AVG(amount) AS customer_avg
  FROM orders
  WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT p.customer_id, p.customer_avg, g.avg_amount
FROM per_customer p, global_avg g
WHERE p.customer_avg > g.avg_amount
ORDER BY p.customer_id;

steps.title: Name the input
steps.body: orders is a CTE built from VALUES: a small table you can read in every later step.

steps.title: One value for everyone
steps.body: global_avg has exactly one row: the average of all non-NULL amounts (44).

steps.title: One row per customer
steps.body: per_customer groups by customer_id: its grain is one row per customer.

steps.title: Compare
steps.body: Joining a one-row CTE to every customer row adds the global average as a column; WHERE keeps A (50) and C (90).

lessons.title: UNION, INTERSECT and EXCEPT
lessons.summary: Stack and compare result sets by position: keep duplicates with UNION ALL, compare key lists with EXCEPT, and reconcile two systems.

blocks.title: Columns match by position
blocks.body: A set operation combines two SELECTs with the same number of columns. Columns are matched by position, not by name, and the result takes its names from the first SELECT. Cast both sides to the same type when they differ. DuckDB also offers UNION BY NAME, which matches columns by name.

blocks.title: UNION removes duplicates
blocks.body: UNION is UNION ALL followed by DISTINCT over whole rows: two genuine total rows with the same label and amount collapse into one. Use UNION ALL unless removing duplicates is the point, and then say so in a comment.

blocks.title: Comparing two lists
blocks.body: a EXCEPT b returns the distinct rows of a that are not in b; INTERSECT returns the distinct rows found in both. Unlike NOT IN, both treat two NULLs as the same value. To label every key of a reconciliation (matched, source only, target only) in one pass, use a FULL OUTER JOIN on the key.

blocks.title: Before you run
blocks.body: Predict the row count of UNION ALL and of UNION, then which ids EXCEPT returns in each direction.

code.source:
WITH source(id) AS (VALUES (1), (2), (2), (3), (NULL)),
target(id) AS (VALUES (2), (3), (4), (NULL))
SELECT 'union all' AS operation, COUNT(*) AS row_count FROM (SELECT id FROM source UNION ALL SELECT id FROM target)
UNION ALL
SELECT 'union', COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT id FROM source UNION SELECT id FROM target)
UNION ALL
SELECT 'source except target', COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT id FROM source EXCEPT SELECT id FROM target)
UNION ALL
SELECT 'target except source', COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT id FROM target EXCEPT SELECT id FROM source)
UNION ALL
SELECT 'intersect', COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT id FROM source INTERSECT SELECT id FROM target);

steps.title: Stack with UNION ALL
steps.body: All 9 rows survive, duplicates and NULLs included.

steps.title: Remove duplicates with UNION
steps.body: Distinct rows only: 1, 2, 3, 4 and one NULL, so 5 rows.

steps.title: Compare with EXCEPT
steps.body: source EXCEPT target keeps 1; target EXCEPT source keeps 4. The two NULLs count as equal.

steps.title: Keep the common rows
steps.body: INTERSECT keeps 2, 3 and NULL: 3 distinct rows.
